lessons.title: Understanding a selected story
lessons.html:
Understanding a selected story

In this unit you read texts chosen for you, such as a short story, a poem or a song, and you show that you understand them and can say what you think. Here is a short story to practise with.

The Night Shift

Mpho had worked in the broiler houses for six years. She knew the sound of healthy chickens: a soft, busy noise, like a market far away. On the night of the storm the power went off. The fans stopped. The house grew hot and quiet. Mpho's new partner, Johan, wanted to wait for the manager. "It is not our job," he said. Mpho did not answer. She ran to the generator shed, started the generator the way she had been trained, and opened the side curtains. By the time the manager arrived, the soft busy noise was back. The manager looked at Johan. Johan looked at the floor. "Next time," he said quietly, "show me how."

Understanding the story

  • Characters: Mpho, an experienced worker; Johan, a new worker; the manager.
  • Setting: a poultry farm, at night, during a storm.
  • Conflict: the power fails and the chickens are in danger from heat. Mpho and Johan disagree about what to do.
  • Climax: Mpho starts the generator.
  • Ending: the chickens are safe and Johan asks to learn.

Reading between the lines

Writers do not always tell us everything. We work some things out from clues. This is called inference.

  • Why does Mpho not answer Johan? She knows there is no time to argue. Her actions answer him.
  • Why does Johan look at the floor? He is ashamed.
  • What does show me how tell us? Johan has changed. He wants to take responsibility.

lessons.title: Giving and supporting your response
lessons.html:
Giving and supporting your response

The writer's choices

Think about why the writer made certain choices:

  • The story starts and ends with the sound of the chickens. This frames the story and shows that all is well again.
  • The comparison like a market far away helps us hear the sound.
  • Short sentences, such as The fans stopped, make the scene feel tense and fast.
  • The title The Night Shift is simple, but the shift is also a change in Johan.

Themes

  • Responsibility: doing what is needed, not only what is in your job description.
  • Experience and training: Mpho could act because she was trained.
  • Learning: a person can change after a mistake.

Writing a response

A good written response has three parts:

  1. Main idea: I think the story is about taking responsibility at work.
  2. Evidence: Mpho does not wait; she runs to the generator. Johan says it is not our job, but at the end he asks to be shown how.
  3. Your view and link: I agree with the writer. On our farm, when the borehole pump failed, my supervisor fixed the problem first and reported after.

Talking about texts in a group

  • Take turns. Let each person finish.
  • Say I think... because... rather than you are wrong.
  • Ask questions: why do you say that? Where in the story do you see it?
  • You may change your mind after hearing a good reason.

Comparing texts

You may read two texts on the same theme, such as a poem about drought and a story about a flood. Compare: what is the same, what is different, and which one moved you more and why.

Key points

  • Identify characters, setting, conflict, climax and ending.
  • Use clues in the text to work out what is not said directly.
  • Notice the writer's choices, like comparisons and short sentences.
  • Support every opinion with evidence from the text.
  • Discuss respectfully and be open to other views.
